# Same-model review

## Correctness
**PASS.** The final claim was reconstructed from the canonical realization of the Fremlin tensor as the vector sublattice generated by the algebraic tensor. A finite lattice representation gives finitely many algebraic branches; Baire category forces one branch on an open rectangle. The local section span is finite-dimensional. Choosing a section basis and evaluation points with invertible matrix gives analytic coefficient functions, and the real-analytic identity theorem propagates the local separated representation across the connected interior. Continuity then handles the boundary. The zero local-rank case is included. No numerical evidence is used as proof.

## Originality
**PASS, with stated residual risk.** The focal full text, arXiv:2609.33963v1, proves only the nonmembership of \((s,t)\mapsto e^{st}\) and uses a Wronskian after finding one finite-rank rectangle. The final claim instead classifies every interior-real-analytic member of the tensor. Targeted published-finding searches covered analytic kernel, local finite rank, finite separation rank, Riesz/Fremlin tensor, and algebraic-tensor formulations, and current/prior owned ledgers were checked for the source and these aliases. No covering statement was found.

The closest broader literature is Fremlin--Talagrand's decomposition theorem and Grobler--Labuschagne's approximation paper. Only abstract/bibliographic material was available in the inspected paths for those comparators, so an older equivalent corollary under different terminology remains a residual originality risk. Azouzi--Ben Amor--Jaber and Buskes--Wickstead address algebra structures rather than this analytic membership classification.

## Value
**PASS.** The result converts the source's kernel-specific obstruction into an exact structural boundary: on the real-analytic slice, Fremlin tensor membership is equivalent to finite separation rank. This yields a reusable exclusion criterion for analytic kernels and explains why the source's \(e^{st}\) example is one instance of a larger phenomenon. The statement is neither an arbitrary parameter slice nor a routine numerical refinement.

## Closest literature and limitations
The principal scientific anchor is Ben Amor, arXiv:2609.33963v1, especially Section 2 and Lemma 2.2. Broader comparators are Fremlin (1972), Fremlin--Talagrand (1979), Grobler--Labuschagne (1989), and Azouzi--Ben Amor--Jaber (2018). The theorem is limited to \(C([0,1])\mathbin{\bar{\otimes}}C([0,1])\) and kernels real-analytic on the connected interior; it gives no quantitative minimal-rank bound and no conclusion for merely smooth kernels or completed tensor norms.

Same-model review: passed. Independent audit: not yet performed.
